item.title: Constrained UI Components for AI Assembly and Human Review
item.description: A practical method for building UI with coding agents through constrained components, source-based migration contracts, executable assembly recipes, and a reviewable showroom.
item.content:encoded:
I wanted a coding agent to assemble an interface without making a fresh decision about fonts, spacing, button shapes, and animation every time it added a control. I wanted the resulting code to be easier for me to review, too.

My preferred appearance is fairly ordinary: consistent, simple, and predictable. A new settings form should look and behave as though it belongs to the same application. Reviewing it should mostly involve its content, state, and business actions.

That led to a specific boundary in Pith UI: small components with fixed presentation and bounded semantic options. The application assembles those components and connects its own state and callbacks. The extraction shipped in Pith UI 0.6.3 and Pith Desk rc.28 is a useful case study because several earlier attempts got this boundary wrong.

A component library did not preserve the product

I initially asked a coding agent to rebuild the frontend using React and shadcn components. The result covered the main features, but the palette and logo changed, and previously fixed behavior resurfaced. I eventually rolled back that rewrite.

A later attempt exposed a different failure. The library offered smaller parts, and the application still had its callbacks, but the assembled screen lost its centered conversation column, action grouping, compact navigation, and some icons. Individual components looked correct in the showroom while the application layout was broken. The conversation that led to this extraction records both problems.

These were failures in how I specified and accepted the migration. Choosing a component framework had left many application decisions open. Reducing component size had also removed structure that the application still needed.

An established UI contains more specification than a feature list reveals. Its source records which controls share a row, where an error appears, which action remains available during a request, and what happens when an old response arrives after the user switches targets. Those decisions need an explicit home during extraction.

Restrict presentation and keep composition useful

The public component API should describe the choices an application needs to make.

Application choice Library decision
Button label, icon, and action purpose Font, padding, shape, color, and feedback
Value, error, disabled, and read-only state Native control presentation and interaction rules
Children in documented slots Slot structure, alignment, and spacing
Selected item and available options Selection presentation and keyboard behavior
Business callback and target identity Control lifecycle and local pending feedback

For example, this application-local helper uses the 0.6.3 button API:

import {createButtonPart} from 'pith-ui';

export function saveAction(saveDraft: () => Promise<void>) {
  const button = createButtonPart({
    label: 'Save',
    variant: 'primary',
    onAction: saveDraft,
  });

  return {
    part: button,
    setUnavailable(unavailable: boolean) {
      button.update({
        label: 'Save',
        variant: 'primary',
        disabled: unavailable,
      });
    },
  };
}

The returned part can enter a documented parent slot, which then owns its lifetime. The caller has no className, style, padding, font, or animation argument. Local asynchronous pending behavior belongs to the button implementation; the application supplies authoritative availability.

The same restriction must apply to composition. A slot that accepts arbitrary HTML or a native node gives the caller another route to invent its own interface. Pith UI uses opaque part handles and checks that children are genuine library-created parts. Ownership rules reject reusing a part in two parents and retire removed children. These handles do not require an extra DOM wrapper around every existing element. The ownership implementation keeps native nodes private.

This is an API constraint. A host page still controls the browser’s CSS cascade, so the consuming project also needs checks against style overrides and generated-node access. Type declarations guide normal use, runtime validation catches unsupported options, and consumer checks enforce the agreed boundary.

Prove that the parts can express the existing interface

My first small-parts migration assumed that a stack and a toolbar were sufficient layout vocabulary. They were insufficient for the existing screen. The missing capabilities included a centered reading column, separate action groups, and compact rows.

Removing the old templates before proving their replacements made the application the place where those omissions became visible. The safer order starts with the old implementation.

For each region, I needed to read its template, the relevant CSS cascade, its state updates, and the actual Desk caller together. The frozen contract uses Pith UI 0.2.2 and Desk rc.27 as its baselines. It covers nested dialogs, menus, previews, loading surfaces, and shared behavior as well as the initial workspace.

The old source determines the required structure. Screenshots help find omissions and confirm the result, but they cannot tell me which conversation owns a download or whether a failed save should retain a draft.

I then assembled the old regions internally using only the proposed public parts. Whenever an assembly needed a layout capability that the parts could not express, that was a concrete library gap. It required a bounded capability with a defined purpose. Adding arbitrary CSS to Desk would have hidden the gap and weakened the interface I was trying to establish.

The resulting assembly descriptions include the part tree, construction code, state projection, callbacks, and disposal rules. They are executable documentation. In the 0.6.3 package, those sources were bundled for the consumer to adopt locally, while the export map exposed only the parts entry and its stylesheet. There was no public whole-application or scene entry.

That distinction kept the library responsible for component behavior and the application responsible for assembling its product.

State propagation is part of the assembly

A resource editor exposed one of the easiest details to miss.

The old editor’s Save button participated in a shared availability updater. That updater selected controls by internal markers and applied global, conversation, workspace, or active-target availability. Reading only the editor constructor would miss part of its behavior. The dependency lived outside the component being extracted.

The replacement therefore needed more than an initial disabled value. The application had to retain the open editor’s target and project later availability changes into its state. Its local coordinator does that explicitly; the editor assembly applies the additional Save restriction while retaining the established editing and Delete rules.

This matters because availability has several owners. A button may have a local request pending while the host sends a new snapshot. That snapshot must not accidentally re-enable the action. Conversely, a broad rule that disables every control during host activity can change behavior that was intentionally available.

Target changes introduce another boundary. A request started for one resource must not update or close the editor that replaced it. Ordinary state updates should preserve current input; changing the target may require an explicit reset or a new owned instance. Disposal needs to invalidate late callbacks as well as remove visible elements.

For extraction work, I now trace these paths before adding more tests. Existing correct assertions remain the baseline. A focused regression is useful when it captures an actual omitted state transition. A growing test count cannot compensate for an assembly that no longer forwards the old state.

Give the agent and reviewer the same catalog

The showroom is part of the public contract. If it displays internal implementation fragments alongside supported components, a coding agent or developer can reasonably choose something that the application is not allowed to use.

For this extraction, the public showroom was reduced to formal parts, their specifications, legal states, and interactions. Large application assemblies remained in internal validation and assembly documentation.

flowchart TD
    PARTS[Reviewed component implementations] --> CATALOG["Public catalog<br/>and typed API"]
    CATALOG --> AI["AI selects parts<br/>and assembles"]
    CATALOG --> HUMAN["Human reviews states<br/>and interactions"]
    AI --> APP["Application composition<br/>and business wiring"]
    HUMAN --> APP

The package’s short AI guide explains how to choose parts, compose ownership, update state, and release the tree. Its API reference supplies the detailed types. Assembly recipes show how those rules reconstruct a real region.

These need to agree. A convincing screenshot with an example that does not compile is a poor guide for an agent. A compiling example that depends on an unexported helper is also unusable by a real consumer. The package verification compiled the recipes and documentation examples from an independently installed tarball, using the package’s actual public surface.

A missing capability now has a visible route: identify the required native behavior or layout, add the smallest useful library capability, review its legal states, and publish it. Application code can then consume that reviewed version.

Review the decisions at their owning layer

The useful review boundary follows the kind of change.

When a part changes, I review its visual and interaction contract in the library: typography, spacing, icons, focus, keyboard behavior, pending and error states, and lifecycle. A change there can affect many screens, so its supported variants need inspection together.

When an application composition changes, the review centers on a smaller set of questions:

  • Does the part tree preserve the required grouping, order, and slots?
  • Do labels, action purposes, and error locations communicate the right meaning?
  • Does each callback retain the correct target and revision?
  • Are updates, resets, replacement openings, and destruction connected correctly?
  • Does the application stay within the public parts API?

Visual inspection still matters. The intended benefit is that a composition change introduces fewer independent visual decisions. I can follow the arrangement and business wiring without also accepting a new set of local font sizes and CSS exceptions.

This gives AI a more specific task as well. It can select approved parts, supply content and state, connect callbacks, and compose a documented tree. A request for a different spacing rule becomes a library change that can be reviewed where that rule is owned.

What the migration established

The coverage map connects 36 old regions to assembly sources and behavior checks. The published 0.6.3 package included 32 compiling assembly sources and 33 compiling documentation examples.

After verifying the published package, Desk installed that exact npm version and adopted the assemblies. The migration commit preserved the existing business controller bodies, host boundary, configuration, conversations, palette, and logo. It introduced no copied legacy HTML/CSS or application style overrides.

Behavior checks ran in Chromium and WebKit. Across 56 comparison scenarios, the captured geometry and style values matched the baseline. Forty-nine screenshots were pixel-identical; the remaining differences were small Chromium antialiasing variations. That establishes the result of this migration. It leaves long-term maintenance savings to be judged through subsequent changes.

The approach has costs. Missing variants require library work. Too many narrowly named parts can make the catalog hard to navigate. Application-local recipes can also accumulate duplication, and a helper that merely forwards arguments may add little value. I would keep checking whether each boundary captures a repeated rule or an important behavior.

For a product with an established visual language, I prefer making those rules explicit. The library gives both the coding agent and the reviewer a finite vocabulary. The application code then shows how that vocabulary is used to express the product’s state and actions.

item.title: From One-Time Porting to Incremental Updates: Portsmith Go and Pith
item.description: A field report on using a Go port of Pi to execute its own upstream updates, with concrete commits, independent acceptance records, and the limits of the bootstrap.
item.content:encoded:
I used Pi to help port selected Pi components from TypeScript to Go. Then I used the resulting Go SDK, Pith, to power the tool that performs later Pi-to-Pith updates.

That second part was the experiment I wanted to run after the first migration. Translating a pinned version gives you a starting point. Upstream keeps changing, and the Go implementation acquires its own callers, tests, and design choices. How do you update it without treating every release as another rewrite?

My first report covered the initial migration: a TypeScript workbench called Portsmith, powered by Pi Coding Agent, accepted 26 steps across AI, agent core, and tools. It ended with a plan to let Pith help maintain Pith. This follow-up covers the Go executor and two accepted upstream increments that followed.

The result is a bootstrapped maintenance workflow. Pith runs the implementation agent inside Portsmith Go; Portsmith Go checks and integrates updates to Pith. A developer or an external coding assistant still prepares and reviews the behavior contracts and acceptance tests.

Moving the migration executor to Pith

Portsmith Go is a Go port of the original migration workbench. Its original acceptance receipt records seven accepted steps, delivered in commit 710f8b9. The original TypeScript executor produced that port. Incremental sync and integration repair were subsequent native Go additions.

The important change is in the execution backend. In agent.go, RunPort opens a durable Pith session, constructs a tool registry, and calls codingagent.CreateAgentSession. It supplies the selected model, resources, session manager, and retry and compaction policy. This is a library call inside the Go process.

The agent gets Pith’s native read, write, edit, shell, and search tools, plus Portsmith’s verify_candidate tool. It can implement a candidate, receive compiler and independent-test diagnostics, and repair the code in the same conversation. Portsmith owns acceptance, integration, and commits. The agent’s final message is not the acceptance decision.

flowchart TD
    PI[Upstream Pi revisions] --> REVIEW[Reviewed increment and frozen tests]
    REVIEW --> GO[Portsmith Go]
    PITH[Pith Go SDK] -->|Runs implementation agent| GO
    GO -->|Verifies and integrates updates| PITH

This is the bootstrap: the migrated runtime becomes a dependency of the tool that updates that runtime. It also creates a practical version boundary. Portsmith Go links a pinned Pith revision through go.mod; accepting new Pith source does not replace the executor already running. Updating the consumer’s dependency and rebuilding it is a separate step.

The Go product runs without a Node or Pi installation. It still needs Go and Git to compile, verify, and integrate target projects. Its TypeScript analyzer embeds the TypeScript compiler in Goja, a JavaScript interpreter implemented in Go. The analyzer has not itself been rewritten as a Go TypeScript compiler.

Two accepted upstream increments

The Pith history contains two useful milestones after the initial port. Dates below use Singapore time, UTC+8.

Accepted commit Date Upstream revision Scope
0044a03 October 1, 2026 002fc8385268 Three steps for provider stream events, agent observation, and SDK observation
2f7f735 October 3, 2026 a13d35a742c6 Nine steps for the selected Pi 1.0 SDK capabilities

The first increment exercised the route from provider adapters through the agent and into the embedded SDK. Its receipt identifies portsmith-native-go-v1 as the verifier. It was already using the native Go workflow.

The Pi 1.0 increment expanded the scope substantially. Its reviewed plan covered model foundations and catalogs, model operations, streaming protocols, authentication, agent core, MCP, Codemode, SDK integration, and delivery.

The workflow authorized changes to 234 existing files, kept 815 baseline files read-only, and named 26 independent acceptance tests across nine steps. Those counts describe the prepared scope: they are not a count of files actually changed or proof that every upstream behavior was covered.

The final receipt records all nine steps. Both increment receipts report successful compilation, vet, candidate tests, and independent behavior tests. Both retain fullParityProven: false. Unlike the original Portsmith Go port receipt, these two final increment receipts do not list a race phase.

The accepted code commit and the upstream-baseline commit are distinct. After the Pi 1.0 module was accepted, a569953 advanced the tracked revision. This distinction matters when execution is interrupted between delivering code and recording the next starting point.

Finding the Go code affected by an upstream change

An incremental port needs more than a diff. A TypeScript file may map to several Go packages, and a shared type change can affect code that upstream did not edit directly.

Portsmith Go keeps explicit source ownership: each watched TypeScript source maps to its Go outputs. Initialization imports existing migration records and source maps; that ownership is reviewed and committed before preparing a new increment. Reference-only inputs are tracked separately so that a changed reference does not automatically authorize edits to unrelated implementation files.

The sync implementation analyzes both the old and new source trees and builds a reverse import graph. It starts with changed sources and follows their dependents. Looking at both revisions matters for removed imports and deleted files. Configuration JSON changes conservatively include all mapped source.

That produces a draft containing exact changes, affected sources, unmapped inputs, and proposed Go output ownership. It makes no model calls at this stage. A reviewer then resolves the semantic questions: which behavior changes, which APIs remain compatible, which new sources need owners, and which upstream changes are outside the chosen SDK scope.

One concrete decision in the Pi 1.0 core contract was to retain Pith’s existing experimental harness and compatibility APIs even though upstream had removed its harness. Upstream deletion did not authorize deleting APIs already exposed by the Go library. Durable was deferred from this particular increment.

That is why I want a reviewed migration plan between the diff and the implementation agent. A source dependency graph can identify likely impact. It cannot decide the compatibility policy for downstream applications.

Protecting existing code and acceptance tests

The initial migration mostly created outputs. An increment must replace existing implementation while preserving everything outside its reviewed scope.

Version-2 workflows separate existing files into two sets. baseline.files are frozen dependencies. updates.files are existing files explicitly authorized for replacement. Both are tied to a target Git commit and content hashes. Independent judges, manifests, and historical receipts stay outside the writable update set.

The candidate begins with the authorized original implementation. Other baseline material is available as read-only input. Verification runs the frozen independent tests alongside candidate self-tests; later steps accumulate the earlier acceptance gates. Passing a later step does not allow the implementation agent to weaken an earlier contract.

For Pi 1.0, the acceptance tests ask specific questions: do model identities distinguish operation kinds, do nested tool hooks preserve structured replacements, can MCP transports return the expected content, and does deferred tool activation compose with SDK routing? Those questions are narrow enough to execute. Their value depends on how well the reviewer chose them.

Hashes and ownership checks protect the workflow’s inputs and integration decisions. They do not turn a model-controlled shell into an operating-system sandbox. The executor runs in the local user’s environment.

Repairing a candidate that fails after integration

An isolated candidate can pass its own acceptance suite and still break an existing caller. Portsmith Go gained automatic whole-project integration repair in 8055d84, on October 3, after the Pi 1.0 acceptance commit. This is a later executor improvement, separate from the evidence in those two increment receipts.

When the target project’s regression suite fails, the executor archives the diagnostics and persists a rollback transaction. It restores recorded original files, removes recorded additions, and reopens the final implementation step with the failure as feedback. Earlier accepted checkpoints remain. The repaired candidate must pass cumulative acceptance and the project suite before the module is committed.

The TestWorkflowV2IntegrationFailureRepairsCandidate regression makes this boundary visible. A two-step candidate passes isolated checks but misses a marker required by a historical project test. The deterministic generator adds that marker during repair. The test checks that the first step stays accepted, the historical test is unchanged, the failure report survives, and exactly one module commit is created.

This fixture tests the executor’s recovery behavior without asking a live model to reproduce a particular mistake. A separate Pith backend test drives failure diagnostics, a file repair, successful verification, and session resume through the actual Pith tool loop using a deterministic model stream.

Recovery must also distinguish interrupted work from an external edit. It accepts the recorded old bytes or verified new bytes; an unexpected third hash stops recovery and preserves the edit. Tests cover this refusal and recovery of the separate metadata commit. A recovery mechanism that overwrites unrelated work would be a poor trade for automation.

Trying the workflow

The incremental migration guide documents initialization, ownership, review, execution, and recovery. For a project with a committed sync configuration, the sequence is:

# Build Portsmith Go from its checkout.
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -o bin/portsmith ./cmd/portsmith

# Prepare a draft for a chosen full upstream Git commit.
./bin/portsmith sync --project ../target --upstream <full-upstream-commit>

# Review and complete the draft's ownership, contracts, and independent tests.
# Check the prepared plan without making model calls.
./bin/portsmith sync --project ../target --upstream <full-upstream-commit> --check

# Execute with local provider credentials and commit accepted results.
./bin/portsmith sync --project ../target --upstream <full-upstream-commit> \
  --commit --env-file .env

The default draft preparation exits with code 2 when review is needed. That is an expected preparation state. The execution command resumes from durable progress when repeated; a partial run keeps the old accepted upstream baseline. Git push remains an operator action.

These commands describe the workflow for an existing configured target. Repeating the historical Pi 1.0 run requires the pinned starting tree and reviewed materials, rather than today’s already-updated Pith checkout.

What the bootstrap gives me

The two increments establish something more useful than another successful translation: the Go runtime can execute a real migration tool, and that tool can apply reviewed upstream updates to the runtime itself. Maintenance now has explicit source ownership, acceptance gates, checkpoints, and a recorded starting revision for the next increment.

The same SDK has a separate consumer in Pith Desk. Its run execution code also constructs a Pith agent session directly. Portsmith Go tests the SDK as a migration engine; Desk uses it as a desktop application’s runtime. That makes compatibility decisions consequential beyond the migration repository.

I have included a compact evidence summary with pinned commits, receipt hashes, acceptance phase results, plan counts, and the focused offline checks run for this report. The original receipts and reviewed plans remain linked above. The checks prove the exercised behaviors; neither a complete receipt nor the bootstrap establishes full Pi compatibility or reliable unattended handling of every future change.

The next question for me is how much judgment can be made reusable. Source mappings and recovery can be mechanized. Deciding what a changed upstream behavior should mean for existing Go callers still requires a contract. The useful measure is whether the next reviewed increment can preserve those callers and leave enough evidence to explain why it was accepted.

item.title: Porting Pi to Go: Building Portsmith and Pith
item.description: Why I built a migration workbench, what failed during the first Pi-to-Go port, what the tests and billing dashboard actually show, and the plan to use Pith for future updates.
item.content:encoded:
I wanted an agent runtime I could embed in a product, customize for a customer, and deliver without asking that customer to install Node.js or download npm dependencies. I also wanted to understand the runtime I was shipping.

That led to two projects:

  • Portsmith: a TypeScript-to-Go migration workbench built around the Pi Coding Agent.
  • Pith: the resulting Go port of selected Pi AI, agent-core, and built-in tool capabilities.

The first migration plan is complete: 26 accepted steps across three modules. Pith builds without CGO and produces native command-line programs. That is a useful milestone, but it is not proof of complete Pi compatibility or a production-ready agent.

This is the record of what we built, how we checked it, and where the experiment goes next.

Follow-up, October 14, 2026: From One-Time Porting to Incremental Updates: Portsmith Go and Pith covers the Go executor and two accepted upstream increments that followed this first port.

Why port instead of starting over?

The attraction of Pi was its separation of model access, agent execution, and tools. I did not want to reinvent every streaming edge case or every interaction in an agent loop before I could build a useful product.

Go appealed to me because of its build workflow and distribution model. A compiled Go program can be a convenient artifact for a server or a user’s computer. That does not eliminate operating-system differences, and a shell tool still needs a shell. It does reduce the runtime setup I need to explain to someone else.

A port also does not have to reproduce every implementation detail. A mature Go library may be a better answer than translating a TypeScript utility line by line. The important questions are which behaviors must remain equivalent, which dependencies are acceptable, and how the differences will be tested.

We pinned Pi to v0.87.1, commit f07218c4d4bbc12bef056a7058c3dd49dfe41abe. The scope was deliberately narrower than the entire repository: AI, the selected stable agent core, and built-in tools. TUI, Web UI, desktop packaging, Computer Use, MCP, and experimental/pico3 were not part of this migration.

A plan before a loop

My initial picture was simple: give an agent some TypeScript and ask for Go. The dependency graph made that insufficient almost immediately.

We needed an inventory of source files and exported symbols, a target Go package graph, decisions about third-party libraries, explicit behavior contracts, and tests that were not just written by the same model to approve its own answer.

Portsmith therefore separates planning from execution. A human or an external coding assistant prepares the plan. Portsmith executes reviewed steps, runs verification, records checkpoints, and integrates completed modules.

The migration had three delivery modules, 24 batches, and 26 internal steps:

Module Accepted steps Focus
AI 13 Types, streaming utilities, authentication, models, and provider adapters
Core 7 Contracts, execution loop, resources, sessions, compaction, runtime, and harness
Tools 6 Execution environment, file and shell tools, and SDK/CLI delivery

This gave me a small number of meaningful delivery milestones while keeping each generation task manageable. I did not have to type a separate command for every source file or judge.

Pi needed its coding-agent tools

One early mistake was giving the migration model a restricted set of custom file operations. When the generated Go failed to compile, the model did not have the same practical workflow as a coding agent working in a repository.

We changed Portsmith to embed the full Pi Coding Agent. It retained its native file, edit, search, and Bash tools, persistent conversations, context management, and configured skills/extensions. Portsmith added a verify_candidate tool so the model could receive compiler and test diagnostics, repair the candidate, and try again in the same conversation.

The division of responsibility became much clearer:

  • Pi explores, implements, runs commands, and repairs code.
  • Portsmith checks the frozen materials, runs independent acceptance, records progress, and decides whether a module can be integrated.

A model saying “done” does not create an accepted module. Neither do self-tests alone.

The execution environment is still the local user’s environment. Setting a candidate working directory is not sandboxing. That matters if this approach is applied to untrusted repositories or given access to sensitive credentials.

The failures that improved the tool

The useful lessons came from interruptions rather than from the final success message.

Compiler diagnostics must reach the model. Go’s structured output can include build-output events. Filtering only ordinary test-output events hid the exact compiler error that the model needed. We fixed the diagnostic parser instead of asking the user to patch generated Go by hand.

An arbitrary repair budget can turn automation into babysitting. The initial outer loop stopped after a few failed attempts. We changed the default to continued repair, while keeping explicit budgets available. The same applied to fixed file-count, file-size, and verification-time limits that had been chosen for a small experiment rather than a full migration.

Bookkeeping can fail after the code has passed. The AI module’s cumulative receipt grew to about 1.16 MB. Portsmith then rejected its own report under a 512 KiB source-file limit. The code had already passed; integration bookkeeping was the failure. The pending transaction and file hashes let us resume without regenerating the AI module.

A live process is not necessarily making progress. One overnight stretch was dominated by laptop sleep and request timeouts. Elapsed wall time was a poor proxy for model or compiler speed. This is one reason I am not presenting the run as a clean performance benchmark.

Removing fixed limits did not make failures disappear. Authentication problems, exhausted provider retries, changed inputs, and Git conflicts can still require intervention. Tests can also hang. “Keep going by default” is a policy choice, not a guarantee that a run will finish unattended.

What the completion message proves

The final run reported status: complete and recorded these module commits:

Module Commit
AI a5aeab8214f672d5d83e35fec78bf4d0daf67473
Core adbc36268f0c0cad3f5aad7c591b5f0a18f79ac0
Tools 0d4d1479739fcbe849fec21fc02cf8ac31aee237

The receipts record successful compilation, vet, candidate tests, independent behavior tests, and race checks. They deliberately retain fullParityProven: false.

For release preparation, I also ran a separate check on the completed tree:

  • 963 passing Go test events, with no failures or skips, using CGO_ENABLED=0 on macOS arm64.
  • All packages compiled without CGO for macOS arm64, Linux amd64, and Windows amd64.
  • The native pith --help command ran locally.

Cross-compilation is not a runtime test on those other operating systems. This release check did not make live calls to every provider. A fixed set of judges cannot prove behavior that it does not exercise.

The machine-readable evidence summary includes module receipts, hashes, verification outcomes, and the release checks. Pith keeps the original receipts under migration/results/, along with contracts, judges, and source mappings. Raw agent conversations stay local rather than becoming public artifacts.

Portsmith itself changed during the run, including changes that had not yet been committed at execution time. The earlier Portsmith commit alone is therefore not a reproducible identifier for the whole experiment. Preserving and reviewing those changes is part of preparing the repositories for release.

What the DeepSeek dashboard showed

For September 28–29, 2026, in GMT+7, the DeepSeek dashboard showed:

Metric Dashboard value
Cost ¥30.59 CNY
API requests 2,543
Tokens 345,687,190
Model shown deepseek-flash
API-key filter All

This is account-wide usage for the selected dates, not a separately metered migration invoice. It includes whatever requests were billed to the account in that window, potentially including experiments and retries. It does not include the cost of the external planning assistant or local compute. The dashboard also notes that usage can lag by up to five minutes.

The token total is not the number of unique source-code tokens or generated Go tokens. It is the dashboard’s aggregate usage across requests. The screenshot does not expose a cache-hit/input/output breakdown, so I am not using it to infer one.

The image is a cropped browser screenshot: account balance, profile, and the unrelated lifetime-cost figure are excluded. The date filter, API-key scope, totals, and model label remain visible.

Building the result

The completed checkout can build its command-line programs with:

CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -o ./bin/ ./cmd/...
./bin/pith --help

Normal runtime builds should remain possible without CGO. The race detector is a separate testing concern and enables CGO for instrumentation. I want dependency selection to respect the no-CGO runtime goal, rather than discovering a mandatory C dependency just before shipping.

The current pith CLI is non-interactive and uses an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions path. Having multiple provider packages in the repository does not mean every provider is exposed through that command. Real model calls, tool behavior in actual working directories, and session recovery still deserve hands-on acceptance testing.

Both repositories retain their existing AGPL licenses. Pi-derived material retains upstream MIT attribution. This is an independent project, not an official Pi distribution.

Next: let Pith help maintain Pith

The next experiment is to use Pith itself as the execution backend for future Pi-to-Pith migrations.

The loop I want is periodic rather than a one-off rewrite:

  1. Compare a new pinned Pi revision with the previous source inventory.
  2. Identify affected symbols, packages, tests, and dependencies.
  3. Review an incremental migration plan and update the independent contracts.
  4. Use Pith to perform the port and repair candidates against those tests.
  5. Preserve new receipts and submit the result for review.

That backend and scheduled loop are planned, not implemented. The current Portsmith executor is Pi, and an upstream change can require a design decision rather than a translation.

What I have now is a concrete starting point: a Go runtime, a migration workbench, a completed first plan, and enough evidence to inspect the result. The next question is whether this method can keep the port useful as upstream continues to change.

item.title: AeroPlay: A Flight-Mode Game Hub
item.description: A project note on AeroPlay, a pure frontend offline game hub with mini games, localStorage progress, service worker caching, and add-to-home-screen support.
item.content:encoded:
AeroPlay is a pure-frontend, mobile-first game hub optimized for flight-mode use. It includes small games like Snake, Tetris, 2048, Flappy Bird, Maze, Match-3, Sudoku, and Lights Out.

The whole point is that it should keep working with no network.

Why build it

Airplane mode is a useful product constraint. It removes a lot of lazy assumptions:

  • no backend calls
  • no CDN dependency during play
  • no login
  • no remote save
  • no ads
  • no analytics requirement

What remains is the app itself: local assets, local state, and games that are worth playing in short sessions.

Template shape

AeroPlay is also designed as a template. The repo can be used to bootstrap another offline game hub without carrying old issues or unrelated history.

That makes the project more useful than a single app. It becomes a base pattern:

  • Vite and TypeScript
  • local game modules
  • service worker
  • manifest
  • localStorage progress
  • mobile-first layout

Product boundary

The project should not become a general gaming platform. Its strength is the opposite: a small set of local games, predictable input, and no network requirement.

For this kind of app, “more features” can easily make the experience worse. If the user opens it in flight mode, the app should not show half-broken online features.

What I learned

Offline-first is easiest when it is a requirement from the beginning. Retrofitting offline behavior onto an app that assumed servers and remote assets is much harder.

AeroPlay also shows that simple games still need polish:

  • touch controls
  • stable layout
  • saved state
  • fast startup
  • no accidental scroll
  • clear pause and restart behavior

Those details matter more on a phone than in a desktop demo.

Open source status

AeroPlay is public because it is self-contained, harmless to share, and useful as a template. It is a good example of a small project whose constraints make it more reusable.

item.title: TapSurge: An iPad Tap-Speed Tool Built for Competition Use
item.description: A project note on TapSurge, a Vite and TypeScript tap-speed competition tool designed for iPad, offline use, and raw timestamp export.
item.content:encoded:
TapSurge is an offline-first multi-finger click-speed test for iPad competition use. It is built with Vite, TypeScript, native DOM APIs, and Canvas.

The product sounds tiny: count taps for 10, 30, or 60 seconds. The interesting part is making that count credible.

Why a custom tool

Most tap-speed apps are built for casual play. Competition use has different requirements:

  • work offline
  • run well on an iPad
  • avoid accidental browser gestures
  • count multi-finger input correctly
  • preserve enough raw data to audit a run
  • keep history locally without accounts

For this use case, simplicity matters more than visual novelty.

Input model

TapSurge uses pointerdown and active pointer tracking. The key rule is that holding a finger down should not count repeatedly. A tap is a new press, not a frame, animation event, or repeated touch state.

The app records:

  • total taps
  • average CPS
  • one-second live CPS
  • maximum live CPS
  • maximum simultaneous fingers
  • raw timestamps and pointer IDs

That raw data is important. It lets a run be inspected after the fact instead of trusting only the final number.

Offline design

The app is intended to work in a PWA-like mode. It has a local app shell, a service worker, and no backend dependency during play.

This is one of those projects where offline support is not a nice extra. It is part of the user story. If the tool is used at a booth, in a classroom, or during a small event, network dependency is unnecessary risk.

UI constraints

The UI has to be obvious under pressure. A player should not be reading instructions while the timer is running.

The controls are intentionally few:

  • choose duration
  • start
  • tap
  • see result
  • review history
  • export evidence if needed

The harder work is preventing the browser from interfering: double-tap zoom, scroll gestures, safe-area issues, and fullscreen behavior all matter more on a real iPad than in a desktop browser.

What I learned

Small event tools benefit from being boring. The best version is not the most animated one; it is the one that produces trustworthy results with minimal setup.

TapSurge is a good example of a private tool that could be public, but does not need a large roadmap. Its scope is the feature.
